title: 07. Messaging & Event-Driven Architecture: At Most Once Delivery

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** At-most-once delivery is the guarantee that each message will be delivered zero or one times — the broker sends the message and immediately forgets it, so if the consumer is unavailable, the message processing fails, or the network drops it, the message is silently lost — trading reliability for the lowest possible latency and zero acknowledgment overhead.

At-most-once delivery is the simplest and fastest message-delivery semantic: the producer fires the message at the broker (or directly at the consumer) and immediately moves on, without waiting for an acknowledgment. The broker does not retain the message, the consumer does not ack, and there is no retry on failure. If everything works, the message is delivered once. If anything fails — the broker is down, the network drops the packet, the consumer crashes, the consumer rejects the message — the message is silently lost, with no recovery mechanism. This is "fire-and-forget" semantics, and it is the right choice for a specific class of workloads: high-volume, low-value, time-sensitive data where the cost of missing some messages is acceptable and the cost of acknowledgment overhead (latency, broker storage, retry logic) is prohibitive. The classic examples are metrics, logs, telemetry, and real-time signals — systems where individual messages are low-value, the aggregate is what matters, and stale data (from a delayed redelivery) is worthless anyway. statsd, Statsite, collectd, UDP syslog, and many monitoring pipelines use at-most-once over UDP for this reason.

The mechanics of at-most-once are intentionally minimal. The producer sends the message (via UDP, or via a broker with `acks=0` in Kafka, or via a fire-and-forget HTTP POST) and does not wait for any response. The broker, if present, accepts the message and writes it to the queue or topic, but does not retain it for redelivery — once written, it is the consumer's responsibility to pick it up before retention expires, and if the consumer is slow or absent, the message is dropped. The consumer reads and processes the message but does not ack — if the consumer crashes mid-processing, the message is lost (no redelivery). Kafka's `acks=0` producer setting is the canonical at-most-once producer: the producer does not wait for the broker's acknowledgment, so if the broker is down or the network drops the message, the producer does not know and does not retry. SQS does not natively support at-most-once (it is always at-least-once), but a producer can simulate it by not retrying on failure. UDP-based protocols (statsd, syslog, SNMP traps) are inherently at-most-once because UDP has no acknowledgment or retry.

Real-world systems use at-most-once for high-volume telemetry. statsd, the popular metrics aggregator from Etsy, uses UDP for metric ingestion — each metric is a single UDP packet, and if a packet is dropped, the metric is lost (but the aggregate over time is still statistically valid). Netflix's Atlas metrics pipeline, Datadog's agent, and Prometheus's pushgateway all support at-most-once ingestion for high-volume metrics where losing 0.1% of points is acceptable. Logging pipelines often use at-most-once (e.g., syslog over UDP, or a fire-and-forget HTTP logger) to avoid blocking the application on log delivery — better to lose a log line than to block the request thread. Real-time signal pipelines (gaming tick updates, financial market data feeds, IoT sensor streams) use at-most-once because stale data from a delayed redelivery is worse than a missing data point — the latest reading is what matters, and a 5-second-old reading is useless. The common theme: the value of each individual message is low, the aggregate is what matters, and the latency of acknowledgment would be unacceptable.

The trade-off of at-most-once is stark: you get the lowest possible latency and zero acknowledgment overhead, but you accept silent message loss. Compared to at-least-once, at-most-once eliminates one round-trip per message (the ack) and the broker's retention burden — a producer can fire 100,000 messages per second on a single thread with no waiting, while at-least-once would cap at perhaps 10,000 per second per thread due to ack round-trips. Compared to exactly-once, at-most-once eliminates the dedup table and transactional overhead entirely. The cost is that any failure (broker down, network drop, consumer crash, slow consumer) silently loses messages. For metrics, this is fine — losing 0.1% of metric points does not materially change the aggregate, and the alarm thresholds are set with noise tolerance in mind. For payments or orders, this is catastrophic — losing 0.1% of payments is millions of dollars per year. The architect's rule: use at-most-once only for low-value, high-volume, time-sensitive data where loss is tolerable; never use it for anything where each individual message matters.

A subtle but important aspect of at-most-once is the consumer-side behavior. In at-most-once, the consumer typically auto-acks on receive (or does not ack at all — fire-and-forget on both sides). This means if the consumer crashes mid-processing, the message is lost. For some workloads this is fine (e.g., a metrics aggregator that loses a few points on crash); for others it is a bug (e.g., a log pipeline that drops logs on consumer restart). The fix for the latter case is to make the consumer's processing idempotent and fast — if processing is a quick in-memory aggregation (e.g., incrementing a counter), the window for crash-induced loss is tiny. For more complex processing, the architect should consider whether at-most-once is really the right choice, or whether a hybrid approach (at-most-once for ingestion, at-least-once for downstream processing) would be better. Many real-world pipelines use at-most-once for the high-volume ingestion hop (e.g., UDP -> statsd) and at-least-once for the downstream aggregation hop (e.g., statsd -> graphite -> alerting), getting the best of both worlds: low-latency ingestion with no ack overhead, and reliable downstream processing.

The failure modes of at-most-once are well-understood and the system must be designed around them. (1) **Producer-broker failures**: if the producer fires a message and the broker is down, the message is lost. Mitigation: monitor broker availability and alert on producer send failures (if exposed — UDP producers often cannot even detect failures). (2) **Network drops**: UDP packets can be dropped by the network under congestion. Mitigation: monitor packet loss rates and provision enough bandwidth; consider TCP-based at-most-once (e.g., HTTP fire-and-forget) if loss is too high. (3) **Consumer crashes**: if the consumer crashes mid-processing, the message is lost. Mitigation: keep processing fast and idempotent; minimize the crash window. (4) **Slow consumers**: if the consumer cannot keep up, the broker's buffer fills and either drops new messages (most common) or applies backpressure. Mitigation: provision enough consumer capacity; monitor consumer lag; use a buffer-overflow strategy (drop oldest, drop newest, or drop random) explicitly. (5) **No deduplication**: at-most-once producers can sometimes send duplicates if they retry (e.g., a TCP-based producer that times out and retries, but the original actually went through). The architect must decide whether the consumer is idempotent or whether duplicates are acceptable. For most at-most-once workloads (metrics, logs), duplicates are tolerable noise; for some (alerts triggered on thresholds), duplicates can cause false alarms.

### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    P[Producer] -->|send msg, no ack wait| B[Broker]
    B -->|deliver, no ack required| C[Consumer]
    P -.->|"if broker down: msg LOST"| LOST((LOST))
    B -.->|"if consumer slow: msg DROPPED"| DROPPED((DROPPED))
    C -.->|"if consumer crashes: msg LOST"| LOST
    style P fill:#dfd
    style B fill:#ffd
    style C fill:#dfd
    style LOST fill:#fdd,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
    style DROPPED fill:#fdd,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
   +-------+    send msg (no ack wait)    +---------+
   | Prod  |----------------------------->|         |
   +-------+   (fire-and-forget)          | Broker  |
       |                                  |  (queue)|
       | if broker down: msg LOST         +----+----+
       |                                       |
       |                                  deliver (no ack)
       |                                       |
       |                                       v
       |                                  +---------+
       |                                  |Consumer |
       |                                  |         |
       |                                  +----+----+
       |                                       |
       |                       if slow: buffer overflow -> DROPPED
       |                       if crash mid-process: msg LOST
       |
       (no retry, no redelivery, no dedup table)
```

### Walkthrough
1. The producer sends the message to the broker with `acks=0` (or over UDP) — it does not wait for a response and immediately moves on to the next message. If the broker is down or the network drops the packet, the message is silently lost; the producer does not know and does not retry.
2. The broker accepts the message and makes it available to the consumer, but does not retain it for redelivery. The consumer reads the message and processes it without sending an ack — if the consumer crashes mid-processing, the message is lost (no redelivery).
3. If the consumer is slow and the broker's buffer overflows, new messages are dropped (the drop strategy is configurable: drop oldest, drop newest, or drop random). The system is optimized for low latency and high throughput at the cost of occasional message loss.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
import socket
import random
import threading
import time
from collections import deque

class AtMostOnceProducer:
    """Fire-and-forget producer: send and immediately move on, no ack."""
    def __init__(self, broker_addr=("127.0.0.1", 9999)):
        self.addr = broker_addr
        self.sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)  # UDP
        self.sent = 0
        self.lost = 0  # we can't truly know; this is "send failures detected"

    def send(self, msg):
        try:
            self.sock.sendto(msg.encode(), self.addr)
            self.sent += 1
        except Exception as e:
            # UDP send rarely fails, but if it does, we just drop and move on
            self.lost += 1

class AtMostOnceBroker:
    """In-memory broker with a bounded buffer; drops on overflow."""
    def __init__(self, host="127.0.0.1", port=9999, buffer_size=100):
        self.buffer = deque(maxlen=buffer_size)  # drops oldest on overflow
        self.dropped = 0
        self.sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
        self.sock.bind((host, port))
        self.running = False
        self.thread = None

    def start(self):
        self.running = True
        self.thread = threading.Thread(target=self._recv_loop, daemon=True)
        self.thread.start()

    def _recv_loop(self):
        while self.running:
            try:
                data, _ = self.sock.recvfrom(4096)
                if len(self.buffer) == self.buffer.maxlen:
                    self.dropped += 1
                self.buffer.append(data.decode())
            except Exception:
                pass  # drop silently

    def consume(self):
        if self.buffer:
            return self.buffer.popleft()
        return None

    def stop(self):
        self.running = False
        self.sock.close()

# Demo
broker = AtMostOnceBroker(buffer_size=5)
broker.start()
time.sleep(0.1)  # let it bind

producer = AtMostOnceProducer()
# Send 20 messages into a buffer that holds 5 -> 15 dropped
for i in range(20):
    producer.send(f"metric-{i}")

time.sleep(0.2)
print(f"Producer sent: {producer.sent}, lost: {producer.lost}")
print(f"Broker dropped on overflow: {broker.dropped}")

print("\nConsumer draining buffer:")
while True:
    msg = broker.consume()
    if not msg:
        break
    # Consumer processes without ack; if it crashes here, msg is LOST
    print(f"  processed: {msg}")

broker.stop()
print(f"\nResult: 20 sent, {broker.dropped} dropped on overflow, only 5 processed")
```

quiz.explanation: UDP is the natural transport for at-most-once because it is connectionless, has no built-in acknowledgment or retry, and has minimal per-packet overhead — a single UDP send is essentially a syscall and a network push, with no round-trip. This allows producers to fire hundreds of thousands of messages per second on a single thread. UDP is used by statsd, syslog, SNMP traps, collectd, and many monitoring pipelines.
